chapters.title: What Science Is and How It Works
chapters.goal: understand how scientists generate trustworthy knowledge
chapters.content:
Chapter 1 — What Science Is and How It Works

Goal: understand how scientists generate trustworthy knowledge. Needs first: nothing. Produces: the mental model that the rest of the guide is built on.

1.1 What Science Is

1.1.1 Definition

Science is the pursuit and application of knowledge about the natural and social world, using a systematic method based on evidence.

1.1.2 The key word: empirical

Empirical = known through observation or experiment.

• Not empirical: “Everyone knows garlic boosts immunity” (folk belief); “A bigger dose should work better” (logic without data); “My professor said so” (authority).

• Empirical: “In a controlled trial, group A receiving compound X showed 30% higher antibody titer than the placebo group (p < 0.05).”

1.1.3 What science is not

Opinion, tradition, or a claim no experiment could ever disprove.

1.2 Two Ways of Reasoning

	Inductive	Deductive

Direction	Specific observations → general pattern	General principle → specific prediction

Used for	Generating a hypothesis	Testing a hypothesis

Example	“Every hot-spring sample showed enzyme activity above 55°C → hot-spring bacteria may produce thermostable enzymes”	“If stability comes from disulfide bonds, removing them should reduce stability”

1.3 The Scientific Method — Eight Steps

Observe → Question → Hypothesize → Design → Collect → Analyze → Conclude → Communicate

   ↑___________________________ (new questions loop back) _______________________________|

Step	What you do	How, in practice	Typical mistake

1. Observe	Notice something unexplained	Read recent literature; notice a real-world problem; compare two studies that disagree	Observing nothing specific (“biology is interesting”)

2. Question	Turn it into one specific question	Use the template in §9.2	Question too broad

3. Hypothesize	Predict the answer, testably	SMART + falsifiable (§9.3)	No number, not testable

4. Design	Plan the test in advance	Variables, controls, replicates (§1.5)	No control group

5. Collect	Run it by an SOP	Record raw data as you go; note every deviation	Writing data up from memory

6. Analyze	Find what the data show	Descriptive stats → test → graph (§2.2)	Concluding from one trial

7. Conclude	State only what data support	Stay within tested conditions	Claiming “proof” or extrapolating

8. Communicate	Write it up; peer review	Paper structure (§3.1)	Vague methods nobody can repeat

Practical tip: keep an “odd things” notebook while you read — it becomes your idea bank for Step 1.

1.4 What Makes the Process Rigorous

Principle	Meaning	Why it matters	What breaks it

Objectivity	Report what happened, not what you hoped	Removes bias	Cherry-picking data

Reproducibility	Anyone following your SOP gets the same result	Shows the result is real	Incomplete methods

Statistical validation	Use tests to separate pattern from noise	Prevents false conclusions	One unreplicated trial

Peer review	Independent experts check the work	Catches errors	Skipping review

1.5 Experimental Design Basics

1.5.1 The building blocks

Term	Meaning	Example (enzyme heat stability)

Independent variable	What you change	Temperature (40–70 °C)

Dependent variable	What you measure	Residual enzyme activity

Controlled variables	Kept constant	pH, buffer, enzyme concentration, time

Positive control	Known to give a result → proves the assay works	A commercial heat-stable enzyme

Negative control	Known to give none → proves you are not detecting noise	Buffer with no enzyme

Replicate	Repeat of the same condition	Triplicate tubes

Sample size	Number of independent units	3 independent preparations

1.5.2 Technical vs. biological replicates

•	Technical replicate: same sample measured several times (tests pipetting/instrument consistency).

•	Biological replicate: independently prepared samples (tests whether the effect is real in biology). Reviewers want biological replicates for claims of effect.

1.5.3 Reducing bias

•	Randomization — assign samples to conditions by chance.

•	Blinding — the person measuring does not know which sample is which, where possible.

•	Pre-defining the analysis before seeing the data.

1.5.4 Common mistakes

No negative control; replicates that are all technical; changing two variables at once; deciding the analysis after seeing the data.

Chapter 1 Checklist

•	☐ I can define empirical.

•	☐ I can list the eight steps and say what each produces.

•	☐ I can name the independent, dependent, and controlled variables in an experiment.

•	☐ I know why a negative control is needed.

chapters.title: Essential Vocabulary and Statistics
chapters.goal: be able to read and write biotechnology text without being blocked by terms or numbers
chapters.content:
Chapter 2 — Essential Vocabulary and Statistics

Goal: be able to read and write biotechnology text without being blocked by terms or numbers. Needs first: Chapter 1. Produces: working vocabulary; ability to choose and report a basic statistical test.

2.1 Biotechnology Vocabulary

2.1.1 Molecular tools

Term	Plain meaning

Gene	A DNA segment that carries instructions for a product (usually a protein)

Gene expression	A gene being “read” and turned into its product

Vector / plasmid	A DNA carrier (often a small circular DNA) used to move a gene into a host

Construct	Engineered DNA ready for use (e.g., vector + your gene)

Primer	Short DNA piece that starts copying in PCR

PCR	Technique that copies a chosen DNA region millions of times

qPCR / RT-qPCR	PCR that measures how much DNA (or RNA, after conversion) is present

Knockout	Disabling a gene to see what is lost

CRISPR	Programmable system for cutting or detecting specific DNA

Guide RNA (gRNA)	RNA that directs CRISPR to its target sequence

Mutagenesis	Deliberately changing DNA sequence

2.1.2 Organisms and systems

Term	Plain meaning

Chassis / host organism	The living cell that carries and runs your construct (e.g., E. coli, yeast)

Wild type	The natural, unmodified version — your baseline

Strain / isolate	A specific genetic line of a microbe / a sample-derived microbe

Cell line	Cells grown continuously in the lab

Model organism	A well-studied organism used to stand in for others

2.1.3 Experimental terms

Term	Plain meaning

Assay	A lab test that measures or detects something

In vitro	Outside a living organism (test tube, dish)

In vivo	Inside a living organism

In silico	By computer modelling

Titer	Concentration of something in a sample

Half-life (of activity)	Time for activity to fall to half

Limit of detection	The smallest amount an assay can reliably detect

Specificity / sensitivity	Detects only the target / detects even small amounts of the target

Proof of concept	A small, early study showing an idea can work

2.2 Statistics for Beginners

2.2.1 Describing data

Concept	Meaning

Mean	Average

Median	Middle value (less affected by extreme values)

Standard deviation (SD)	Typical spread of data around the mean

Standard error (SEM)	How precisely the mean is estimated

Range	Lowest to highest value

2.2.2 Judging whether a difference is real

Concept	Meaning	Caution

Null hypothesis (H0)	“No effect/difference”	The thing your test tries to reject

p-value	Probability of seeing a result this extreme if H0 were true	p < 0.05 is a convention, not magic

Statistical significance	Result unlikely under H0	≠ important, ≠ large

Effect size	How big the difference is	Report it, not only p

Confidence interval	Range likely to contain the true value	Wider = less certain

2.2.3 Which test do I use?

Your question	Data	Test

Do two groups differ?	Continuous, roughly normal	t-test

Same samples measured before/after?	Continuous, paired	Paired t-test

Do three or more groups differ?	Continuous, roughly normal	One-way ANOVA (then post-hoc test)

Two factors at once (e.g., temperature × pH)?	Continuous	Two-way ANOVA

Do two measured variables move together?	Continuous	Correlation (Pearson/Spearman)

Does X predict Y?	Continuous	Regression

Do category counts differ (e.g., resistant vs susceptible)?	Counts	Chi-square / Fisher’s exact

Data clearly not normal, small n	Continuous	Non-parametric equivalent (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis)

2.2.4 Sample size and power

Too few replicates → real effects missed. Proposals should state how many replicates and why (a power calculation if possible; otherwise a justified standard such as n = 3 biological replicates).

2.2.5 Three traps

1.	Correlation ≠ causation.

2.	Significant ≠ important.

3.	No significant difference ≠ no difference (you may simply lack power).

2.2.6 How to state statistics in a Methods section

“Data will be reported as mean ± SD of three independent biological replicates. Differences among temperature groups will be analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test, with p < 0.05 considered significant.”

2.3 Reporting Numbers and Units

•	Always give units (µg/mL, °C, h).

•	Give a number of decimals that matches your measurement precision.

•	Label graph axes with variable and unit; show error bars and say what they are (SD or SEM).

Chapter 2 Checklist

•	☐ I can explain vector, chassis, assay, and control in my own words.

•	☐ I know the difference between SD and SEM, and between p-value and effect size.

•	☐ I can pick a test for a two-group and a three-group comparison.

chapters.title: How Research Is Communicated: The Paper
chapters.goal: know the standard structure of a paper, read papers efficiently, and recognize source types
chapters.content:
Chapter 3 — How Research Is Communicated: The Paper

Goal: know the standard structure of a paper, read papers efficiently, and recognize source types. Needs first: Chapters 1–2. Produces: reading skill used in Chapters 7–8; the “skeleton” that proposals transform in Chapter 4.

3.1 Anatomy of a Scientific Paper

#	Section	Job	What goes in it

1	Title	Name the study	Subject + approach, specific

2	Abstract	Whole study in one paragraph	Background, aim, method, key result, conclusion

3	Introduction	Why it matters	Broad context → what is known → gap → aim/hypothesis

4	Methods	Allow reproduction	Materials, organisms, protocols, statistics

5	Results	Report data	Figures/tables + plain description, no interpretation

6	Discussion	Interpret	Compare with literature, limitations, significance

7	Conclusion	Take-home	1–3 sentences, nothing new

8	References	Source list	Consistent style

Remember: Introduction (funnel down to the gap) and Discussion (funnel up from results to meaning) are mirror images.

3.2 How to Read a Paper (You Do Not Read It Top to Bottom)

3.2.1 The three-pass method

Pass	Time	Read	Decide

1. Survey	5 min	Title → abstract → figures/tables → conclusion	Is it relevant?

2. Understand	20–30 min	Introduction → results (with figures)	What did they find, and what gap do they state?

3. Evaluate	As needed	Methods + discussion, critically	Can I trust it? Can I reuse the method?

3.2.2 What to record for every paper

Field	Example

Citation	Author, year, journal

Question/gap they address	…

Their hypothesis	…

Method (one line)	…

Key result (one line, with number)	…

Limitation they state	…

How I might use it	background / method / gap evidence

(This becomes your literature matrix in §7.6.)

3.2.3 Reading tips

•	Write notes in your own words (protects you from plagiarism, §5.1).

•	Look up every unknown term once; add it to your glossary.

•	Don’t expect to understand everything on the first read.

3.3 Types of Sources

Type	What it is	Use it for	Cite it?

Primary research article	Original experiment, peer-reviewed	Evidence, methods, numbers	Yes — the main source type

Review article	Summarizes many studies	Finding gaps, background, finding primary papers	Yes, for background

Systematic review / meta-analysis	Structured, combined analysis	Strong summary evidence	Yes

Preprint	Not yet peer-reviewed	Very recent findings (flag clearly)	Only if allowed

Book / textbook	Established knowledge	Basic concepts	Sparingly

Website / blog / news	Non-scholarly	Orientation only	Generally no

Patent / standard / agency report	Technical, regulatory or market data	Impact and feasibility	Yes, where relevant

Common Mistakes

Reading start-to-finish; copying sentences into notes; citing only reviews; citing a paper without opening it.

Chapter 3 Checklist

•	☐ I can name the eight paper sections and the job of each.

•	☐ I read papers in three passes and keep structured notes.

•	☐ I can tell a primary article from a review.

chapters.title: Paper vs. Proposal, and What Funders Buy
chapters.goal: understand how a proposal differs from a paper and how it is judged
chapters.content:
Chapter 4 — Paper vs. Proposal, and What Funders Buy

Goal: understand how a proposal differs from a paper and how it is judged. Needs first: Chapter 3 (paper skeleton). Produces: the “persuade before you act” mindset that shapes every later chapter.

4.1 The Fundamental Shift

A paper reports research that has happened. A proposal asks for permission and resources to do research that has not happened yet. Timing changes the tense, purpose, audience, and sections.

4.2 Side by Side

	Research paper	Research proposal

Timing	After the work	Before the work

Core question	What did we find?	Why is this urgent, and why will we succeed?

Depth	Full detail of what was done	Justified plan

Audience	Fellow researchers	Funders, supervisors, review boards

Judged on	Rigor of past data	Feasibility, risk, payoff

Money	Already spent	This document requests it

Tense	Past	Future

Sections lost	—	Results, Discussion

Sections gained	—	Timeline, Budget, Impact

A paper proves you were right. A proposal proves you are worth betting on.

4.3 What Funders Actually Buy

Treat a funder as an investor, not a sponsor of curiosity. They buy: 1. Risk reduction — de-risking an unproven mechanism. 2. Practical capability — a tool, assay, vector, or process that clears a real barrier. 3. Stakeholder payoff — a named group that measurably benefits. Test every paragraph: which of these three am I selling here?

4.4 The Five Criteria Reviewers Typically Score

Criterion	Reviewer’s question	Where you answer it

Significance	Does the problem matter?	Problem statement (Ch. 21), Impact (Ch. 26)

Innovation	Is the approach or angle new?	Problem statement, Aims

Approach	Is the plan rigorous?	Methodology (Ch. 23)

Feasibility	Can this team do it with these resources?	Methodology, Timeline, Budget

Impact	What changes if it works?	Impact (Ch. 26)

4.5 Why Proposals Get Rejected

Reason	What the reviewer sees	Fix

Curiosity Fallacy	“Interesting” with no hypothesis or application	Run the So-What test (§8.5)

Fishing expedition	“Collect samples and see” — no hypothesis, no failure threshold	Write a falsifiable hypothesis (§9.3)

Over-scoped	“Cure cancer in 11 weeks for $3,000”	Calibrate scope (§10.2)

Vague aims	Verbs like “explore”	Measurable verbs + numbers

No controls / contingency	Fragile plan	Controls + backup (§23)

Unjustified budget	Round numbers, no link to aims	Map every line to an aim (§25)

Poor reading experience	Dense text, undefined acronyms	Front-load, bold, white space (§10.1)

Chapter 4 Checklist

•	☐ I can state three differences between a paper and a proposal.

•	☐ I can say what funders buy.

•	☐ I know the five scoring criteria.

chapters.title: Academic Integrity, Ethics, and Tools
chapters.goal: know the rules you must follow and the tools that make following them easy
chapters.content:
Chapter 5 — Academic Integrity, Ethics, and Tools

Goal: know the rules you must follow and the tools that make following them easy. Needs first: Chapter 3. Produces: safe note-taking and citation habits; awareness of ethics requirements.

5.1 Plagiarism, Paraphrasing, Quoting

5.1.1 What plagiarism is

Presenting someone else’s words or ideas as your own — intentionally or not. Swapping a few words in a copied sentence is still plagiarism.

5.1.2 How to paraphrase correctly

1.	Read the passage until you understand it.

2.	Close the source.

3.	Write the idea from memory in your own words and structure.

4.	Compare with the original; if phrases match, rewrite.

5.	Cite anyway — paraphrasing removes the words, not the debt.

5.1.3 Quoting

Direct quotes are rare in scientific writing; use only for exact definitions, with quotation marks and a citation.

5.2 Citation Styles

Style	In text	Common in

APA (author-date)	(Smith et al., 2023)	Social/biological sciences

Vancouver (numbered)	[1] or superscript¹	Medicine, biotechnology

Follow your course/funder style consistently; use a reference manager (§5.5).

What needs a citation: established facts from published work, mechanisms, previous findings, comparisons, and claims about gaps and novelty. Your own results are supported by your data and statistics.

5.3 AI Tools

Course rules commonly cap AI-generated text (BT301 materials: ≤25% — confirm with your instructor). Reasons: reviewers want your understanding, and AI can invent citations. Safe uses: grammar or clarity checks on text you wrote. Never cite a paper you have not opened and verified.

5.4 Research Ethics and Biosafety (Why a Proposal Must Mention Them)

Area	Question reviewers ask	What to include

Human samples/data	Is consent and ethical approval planned?	Approval body, consent, anonymization

Animal work	Is it justified, minimized, approved?	Approval, the 3Rs (replace, reduce, refine)

Genetically modified organisms	Is containment adequate?	Biosafety level, containment, disposal

Hazardous chemicals / pathogens	Is risk controlled?	Safety procedures, training

Data	Is data stored and shared responsibly?	Storage, access, privacy

If a project needs none of these, say so in one sentence — silence looks like oversight.

5.5 Tools You Will Use

Tool	Purpose

Google Docs / Word Online	Shared drafting with version history (Team Charter, §11.2)

Zotero / Mendeley	Store sources, insert citations, format reference list

Google Scholar, PubMed	Search (Chapter 7)

Spreadsheet or Gantt tool	Timeline and budget (Chapters 24–25)

Grammar/spell checker	Language pass (§28.3)

Chapter 5 Checklist

•	☐ I take notes in my own words.

•	☐ I know which citation style I must use.

•	☐ I know if my project needs ethics or biosafety approval.

PART B — FINDING AND SHAPING YOUR PROJECT

Now you turn a broad interest into a precise, defensible project. The order matters: you search first, because a gap can only be found in literature; then you narrow through the funnel; then you test whether the result is fundable; then you organize the team that will write it.

Sector → Search literature → Find gap → Question → Hypothesis → Aims → Objectives → Fundability test → Team

chapters.part: PART B — Finding & Shaping Your Project
chapters.goal: pick a field and know who funds it and what they want
chapters.content:
Chapter 6 — Choosing a Sector and Understanding Funders

Goal: pick a field and know who funds it and what they want. Needs first: Chapter 4. Produces: a chosen sector and a target funder framework.

6.1 The Four Biotechnology Sectors

Sector	Focus	Frontier areas	Example priority targets	Typical lab methods

Red (medical)	Human health, diagnostics, therapeutics	Recombinant biologics, nucleic-acid therapeutics, CRISPR diagnostics	Antimicrobial resistance, viral pathogens, cancer biomarkers	Vector construction, expression, ELISA, RT-qPCR, flow cytometry

White (industrial)	Microbial factories, biocatalysis	Thermostable enzymes, metabolic engineering, microbial consortia	Carbon-neutral biomanufacturing, biodegradable polymers	Gibson assembly, CRISPR knockouts, fermentation, enzyme kinetics, HPLC

Green (agricultural)	Crop yield and resilience	Climate-resilient crops, genome-edited plants, bio-inoculants	Food security, less pesticide, saline/arid cultivation	Agrobacterium transformation, stress-gene profiling, fluorescence assays

Blue / Grey (environmental)	Remediation, waste upcycling, marine bioprospecting	Heavy-metal/dye remediation, enzymatic plastic degradation, biosensors	Clean water, circular bioeconomy	Metagenomic screening, co-cultures, degradation assays

6.2 Funding Frameworks

	STDF (Egypt)	ICGEB CRP (International)

Scope	National authority under the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research	International centre (Trieste, New Delhi, Cape Town), 65+ member states

Mechanisms	BARG, Young Researcher Grants, Capacity Building, Graduation Projects	Collaborative Research Programme

Money	Per call	Up to €25,000/year; up to €75,000 over 3 years

Priorities	Egypt Vision 2030: healthcare, agriculture, water treatment, bio-industry	Human health/infectious disease, industrial biotech, agricultural genomics, bioenergy

Structural demands	Work Packages with person-months/deliverables; quantifiable KPIs; direct-cost vs overhead split	Global scientific merit (no duplication of established protocols); verified local infrastructure; training/capacity-building value

(Figures from BT301 course materials — always re-check the current call.)

6.3 Aligning Your Topic with a Funder

1.	List the funder’s stated priorities.

2.	Write one sentence linking your bottleneck to one priority.

3.	If you cannot, choose a different priority — or a different funder.

Pattern across funders: always prove (a) relevance (national priority or international competitiveness) and (b) feasibility (you can deliver with accessible resources).

Chapter 6 Checklist

•	☐ I chose a sector.

•	☐ I can state one funder priority my topic fits.

chapters.title: Searching the Literature
chapters.part: PART B — Finding & Shaping Your Project
chapters.goal: build a reliable, recent, well-recorded body of evidence
chapters.content:
Chapter 7 — Searching the Literature

Goal: build a reliable, recent, well-recorded body of evidence. Needs first: Chapters 3 and 6. Produces: a search log, a literature matrix, and a ≥5-paper seed bibliography.

7.1 Why Search Before You Decide

You cannot claim a gap, justify a hypothesis, or prove feasibility without evidence that you have checked what is known. Reviewers detect superficial literature reviews quickly.

7.2 Where to Search

Source	Best for	Notes

Google Scholar	Broad first pass, citation counts	Includes non-peer-reviewed items; verify

PubMed / PMC	Biomedical and life sciences	Abstracts free; many full texts free

Scopus / Web of Science	Rigorous filtering, citation tracking	Usually university access

ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley	Publisher databases	Via university login

STDF / ICGEB pages	See what funded projects looked like	Required for your funded-study citation

Patent databases	Existing technology	For impact and novelty

7.3 Building a Search, Step by Step

7.3.1 Step 1 — Break the topic into concepts

Topic: rapid detection of colistin-resistant bacteria using CRISPR.

Concept A (organism/problem)	Concept B (technology)	Concept C (purpose)

colistin resistance	CRISPR	detection

mcr-1	Cas12a	diagnostic

Klebsiella pneumoniae	biosensor	point-of-care

7.3.2 Step 2 — List synonyms for each concept

Use the words authors actually use (check how relevant papers phrase it).

7.3.3 Step 3 — Combine with Boolean operators

•	OR between synonyms within a concept (broadens): ("colistin resistance" OR "mcr-1")

•	AND between concepts (narrows): ... AND (CRISPR OR Cas12a) AND (diagnostic* OR detection)

•	NOT to exclude a term (use sparingly).

•	” “ for exact phrases; ***** for word endings (diagnos*).

Full string: ("colistin resistance" OR "mcr-1") AND (CRISPR OR Cas12a) AND (diagnos* OR detection)

7.3.4 Step 4 — Filter

Date 2021–2026 (course rule: ≥60% of citations), article type, language, peer-reviewed.

7.3.5 Step 5 — Adjust

Result	Action

Thousands of hits	Add a concept or narrow terms

Very few hits	Remove a concept, add synonyms, widen dates

Irrelevant hits	Add specific terms or use NOT

7.4 Search Strategies That Save Time

1.	Review first. Find 1–2 recent reviews; they summarize the field and name gaps.

2.	Backward chaining. Read the reference list of a good paper.

3.	Forward chaining. Use “Cited by” to find newer papers.

4.	Author tracking. Search leading authors/labs.

5.	Alerts. Save the search and get new-paper emails.

7.5 Screening and Judging Sources

Question	Why

Peer-reviewed? Check the journal, not just the article	Weeds out unreviewed material

Recent enough (2021–2026 for most)?	Course rule; science moves

Credible journal for this field?	Predatory journals skip real review

Does it support this specific claim?	Related ≠ supportive

Are methods and sample size adequate?	Weak studies mislead

Red flags: no named editorial board, promises of instant publication, no methods detail, claims far beyond the data.

7.6 Recording What You Find

7.6.1 The search log

Date	Database	Search string	Filters	Hits	Useful?

7.6.2 The literature matrix (your most important working tool)

Paper	System/organism	Method	Key result (number)	Limitation stated	Gap suggested	Use in proposal

A filled matrix lets you see contradictions, missing combinations, and untested conditions (§8.3).

7.7 Course Requirements

•	≥ 60% of citations peer-reviewed and published 2021–2026.

•	A 5-paper seed bibliography: validates your organism, vector or assay, plus ≥1 STDF- or ICGEB-funded study in your sector.

•	One consistent citation style (§5.2).

Common Mistakes

Starting with one broad word; no search log; citing from abstracts only; relying only on Google results; collecting papers without a matrix.

Chapter 7 Checklist

•	☐ I built a concept table and a Boolean string.

•	☐ I filtered by date and type.

•	☐ I have a log, a matrix, and ≥5 seed papers.

chapters.title: Finding the Gap
chapters.part: PART B — Finding & Shaping Your Project
chapters.goal: identify a specific, real, worthwhile unknown
chapters.content:
Chapter 8 — Finding the Gap

Goal: identify a specific, real, worthwhile unknown. Needs first: the literature matrix from Chapter 7. Produces: a verified, one-sentence gap statement.

8.1 What a Gap Is

A specific piece of missing or incomplete knowledge, or an unsolved practical problem. Not merely “something nobody studied” — a gap counts only if closing it changes something.

8.2 Types of Gap

Type	Meaning	Example

Contradiction	Studies disagree	Two papers report opposite effects of the same gene

Mechanism	The what is known, the why is not	Salt tolerance observed; responsible gene unknown

Operational bottleneck	A method works but fails at scale/in the field	Assay accurate but needs a centralized lab

Context / population	Solved elsewhere, untested in your strain, crop, region	Fix proven in one crop, untested in local wheat

Method	Current method too slow, costly, or insensitive	24-hour PCR vs. needed 30-minute test

Combination / condition	Factors studied separately, never together	Salinity and heat studied alone, not combined

8.3 Method: Mining the Literature Matrix

1.	Sort the matrix by limitation stated → recurring limitations are gap candidates.

2.	Sort by system/method → look for empty cells (e.g., no one tested condition X in organism Y).

3.	Compare key results → conflicts mean unresolved questions.

4.	Read Future Work / Limitations paragraphs of the newest papers and reviews.

5.	Note explicit gap statements — and check whether a newer paper already closed them.

8.4 How Valuable Is the Gap?

Tier	Example	Verdict

Trivial	“Nobody measured gene X in strain Y at 24 °C”	Zero impact — unknown ≠ worth knowing

Incremental	“Test an existing enzyme on one more crop”	Low priority

Operational bottleneck	“Protein expresses well but triggers immune clearance”	High priority — aim here

8.5 The So-What Test and the Gap Statement

So-What test: If this gap closed tomorrow, who would benefit, and how? No one-sentence answer → keep narrowing.

Gap statement template: > “[Existing approach/knowledge] has achieved [what is known]; however, [specific unresolved problem], which limits [consequence for a named group].”

Example: “Thermostable esterases have been isolated from hot-spring bacteria; however, their long-term stability above 55 °C is undocumented, which limits their adoption in industrial processes.”

8.6 Verify the Gap Is Real

•	☐ Searched ≥3 databases with synonyms.

•	☐ Checked the last 12–24 months for new papers.

•	☐ Checked funded-project databases for the same idea.

•	☐ The claim is “not adequately characterized in context X,” not “nobody ever…”

Common Mistakes

Claiming “no research exists” after one search; picking a gap you cannot afford to test; confusing a topic (“antibiotic resistance”) with a gap.

Chapter 8 Checklist

•	☐ My gap is of the bottleneck/mechanism/context type, not trivial.

•	☐ I passed the So-What test.

•	☐ I verified it is still open.

chapters.title: The Research Funnel: Gap → Question → Hypothesis → Aims → Objectives
chapters.part: PART B — Finding & Shaping Your Project
chapters.goal: convert the gap into a testable, structured plan
chapters.content:
Chapter 9 — The Research Funnel: Gap → Question → Hypothesis → Aims → Objectives

Goal: convert the gap into a testable, structured plan. Needs first: a verified gap (Chapter 8). Produces: one research question, one hypothesis, 2–3 aims, 2–4 objectives per aim, and an alignment table.

9.1 The Funnel at a Glance

GAP                 what is missing            (broad)

 ↓ phrase as a question

RESEARCH QUESTION   what do I want to find out?

 ↓ predict the answer

HYPOTHESIS          what do I predict, testably?

 ↓ decide how to test it

AIMS (2–3)          what will I accomplish?

 ↓ break into steps

OBJECTIVES (2–4/aim) what exact, measurable tasks?   (narrow)

Rule: the funnel never reverses. If objectives are hard to write, the problem is one level up.

9.2 Research Question

9.2.1 What it is

The open question your study answers. It does not predict the answer.

9.2.2 How to write it

1.	Phrase the gap as a question.

2.	Cover one relationship between variables.

3.	Make it answerable with your time, budget, methods.

4.	Templates: “Does [X] affect [Y] under [Z]?” · “What is the effect of [X] on [Y] in [system]?”

9.2.3 The FINER test

Letter	Ask

Feasible	Can I do it with my resources and time?

Interesting	Does it matter to the field?

Novel	Is it not already answered?

Ethical	Can it be done ethically (§5.4)?

Relevant	Does it connect to a funder priority (§6.3)?

Example: “Do esterases isolated from hot-spring bacteria retain catalytic activity after prolonged exposure to temperatures above 55 °C?”

Mistakes: too broad (“How does climate change affect biotechnology?”); already answered; a topic, not a question.

9.3 Hypothesis

9.3.1 What it is

A specific, testable, falsifiable prediction of the answer. Falsifiable = some possible result could prove it wrong.

9.3.2 How to write it

•	SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

•	Template: “If [mechanism], then [predicted outcome with number], because [rationale].”

•	State the direction (increase/decrease), not just “affect.”

Example: “A thermophilic Bacillus esterase (illustrative) retains more than 50% of initial activity after 48 h at 60 °C because of stabilizing disulfide bridges in its catalytic pocket.”

9.3.3 Null and alternative

H0 = no effect; H1 = effect (usually what you state). Your statistical test checks whether H0 can be rejected (§2.2.2).

9.3.4 Weak → strong

Weak	Why	Strong

“The enzyme will be more stable.”	No number	“…retains >50% activity after 48 h at 60 °C.”

“The enzyme might be stable under some conditions.”	Unfalsifiable	State the exact conditions and threshold

“Does gene X affect growth?”	A question	“Knocking out gene X reduces colony growth rate ≥20% within 48 h.”

9.3.5 Not every project tests a hypothesis

Development/engineering projects (building an assay, vector, process) state a performance target instead: “A one-pot assay will detect ≥10 copies/µL within 30 min.” Still specific, measurable, and falsifiable.

9.4 Aims

9.4.1 What an aim is

A broad, verb-led goal describing what you will accomplish to test the hypothesis: “To determine…”, “To construct and verify…”

9.4.2 Aim vs. hypothesis

Hypothesis = a claim. Aim = the action that tests it. One hypothesis → usually 2–3 aims, each from a different angle.

9.4.3 Rules

1.	One aim per major testable component.

2.	Decoupled — if one fails, the others still stand.

3.	Concrete verbs: characterize, construct, quantify, compare, identify. Avoid explore, investigate, study.

4.	Achievable within time and budget.

Example: Aim 1: “To characterize the thermal stability profile of esterase E1 across 40–70 °C.” Aim 2: “To identify structural residues responsible for stability by site-directed mutagenesis.”

Mistakes: one aim only; aim restates the hypothesis; Aim 2 cannot start unless Aim 1 succeeds.

9.5 Objectives

9.5.1 What an objective is

A specific, measurable, time-bound sub-task under an aim. All objectives under an aim, when completed, satisfy that aim.

9.5.2 Aim vs. objective

Aim = destination. Objective = waypoint. Aims: 2–3 total. Objectives: 2–4 per aim.

9.5.3 Rules

SMART · action verb (measure, quantify, compare, clone, sequence) · independently verifiable · together cover the whole aim.

Example (under Aim 1): 1.1 “To measure residual activity of E1 at six temperatures (40–70 °C), in triplicate.” 1.2 “To calculate activity half-life at each temperature using first-order decay kinetics.”

Mistakes: objective that is really an aim; no endpoint (“to study the effect…”); >5 objectives per aim.

9.6 The Five Levels Compared

Level	Answers	Form	Scope	Count	Example

Gap	What is missing?	Statement	Broad	1	Long-term stability above 55 °C undocumented

Research question	What do I want to know?	Open question	One relationship	1	Do these esterases retain activity above 55 °C?

Hypothesis	What do I predict?	Falsifiable claim with number	Specific	1	>50% activity after 48 h at 60 °C

Aim	What will I accomplish?	Verb-led goal	Decoupled	2–3	Characterize stability across 40–70 °C

Objective	What exact tasks?	SMART step	Narrow	2–4 per aim	Measure activity at six temperatures in triplicate

9.7 The Alignment Table (your consistency tool)

Build it now; use it in every later chapter.

Aim	Objective	Method (Ch. 23)	Deliverable	Month	Cost (Ch. 25)

1	1.1 Measure activity at 6 temperatures	Activity assay, triplicate	Stability curve	1–3	Reagents, assay plates

1	1.2 Calculate half-life	First-order kinetics fit	Half-life table	3–4	—

2	2.1 Design mutants	In silico modelling	Mutant list	2–3	Software/none

2	2.2 Express and test mutants	Mutagenesis, expression, assay	Mutant activity data	4–8	Primers, kits

9.8 Two Worked Examples

9.8.1 Example A — Red (diagnostics)

1.	Gap: PCR-based detection of colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae needs centralized labs and ~24 h.

2.	Question: Can a field-deployable assay detect mcr-1 faster than centralized PCR without losing specificity?

3.	Hypothesis/target: A CRISPR-Cas12a one-pot assay detects mcr-1 at ≥10 copies/µL within 30 min with single-nucleotide specificity.

4.	Aims: (1) Design and screen guide RNAs for specificity. (2) Optimize a lyophilized one-pot assay to the stated limit and time.

5.	Objectives (Aim 1): 1.1 Design five candidate gRNAs in silico. 1.2 Screen each against 3 resistant and 3 susceptible isolates.

9.8.2 Example B — Green (agriculture)

1.	Gap: Salinity-tolerant wheat loses yield under combined salinity + heat; the interaction is uncharacterized at gene-expression level.

2.	Question: Does combined stress change salt-tolerance gene expression differently than salinity alone?

3.	Hypothesis: Combined stress reduces HKT1 expression by >40% versus salinity alone at 72 h.

4.	Aims: (1) Quantify HKT1 expression under both conditions. (2) Test correlation with stress markers (e.g., proline).

5.	Objectives (Aim 1): 1.1 Expose seedlings to both conditions in triplicate for 72 h. 1.2 Quantify HKT1 by RT-qPCR normalized to a housekeeping gene.

(Both examples are illustrative.)

9.9 Funnel Quality Check

•	☐ Question has one relationship and ends in “?”.

•	☐ Hypothesis has a number, a direction, and a falsifying result.

•	☐ 2–3 aims, decoupled, measurable verbs.

•	☐ Every objective is checkable and sits under exactly one aim.

•	☐ Alignment table complete.

chapters.content:
Chapter 10 — Is the Idea Fundable?

Goal: test the idea before investing weeks of writing. Needs first: the funnel (Chapter 9). Produces: a go / refine / drop decision and a 5-sentence pitch.

10.1 Know Your Reviewer

•	Senior researchers reading 10–15 proposals in a weekend, tired, skeptical, looking to eliminate weak ones.

•	5-Minute Rule: ~80% of the impression forms from the Abstract and Aims page.

•	Survival rules: front-load the point in each paragraph’s first sentence; bold key terms; use white space and bullets for aims; define every acronym at first use.

10.2 Scope Calibration

Too small	Right-sized	Too large

Trivial gap	One bottleneck, 2 decoupled aims, realistic proof of concept	“Cure glioblastoma in 11 weeks for $3,000”

Reviewer: no impact	Reviewer: fundable, can grow into a larger grant	Reviewer: unrealistic, uninformed

Rule: a fundable grant solves one concrete bottleneck thoroughly.

10.3 The Four Feasibility Pillars

Reviewers do not expect finished data from students; they check you could deliver.

Pillar	What to show

Literature validation	Published work proving your vector/promoter/host/assay works

Biological sourcing	Strains, plasmids, cell lines obtainable (e.g., ATCC, Addgene) at realistic cost

Control architecture	Positive, negative, vehicle controls

Contingency	A backup if the primary construct or assay fails

10.4 The 5-Sentence Test

If you cannot write these five sentences, the idea is not ready.

1.	Burden — In [sector], [problem] causes [quantified cost].

2.	Bottleneck — Current methods rely on [X], which fails because [limitation].

3.	Hypothesis — We hypothesize that [mechanism] will [restore/enhance] [function].

4.	Aims — Aim 1 will [build/verify]; Aim 2 will [evaluate] against [reference standard].

5.	Beneficiary — Success gives [stakeholder] [quantified capability].

10.5 Topic Scorecard (rate 1–5; proceed if no score is below 3)

Criterion	Score

Real operational bottleneck	

Hypothesis falsifiable and numeric	

Feasible with team, lab, budget, time	

Matches a funder priority	

Named beneficiary with quantified benefit	

Ethics/biosafety manageable	

Chapter 10 Checklist

•	☐ Right-sized scope.

•	☐ All four feasibility pillars addressable.

•	☐ 5-sentence pitch written.

•	☐ Scorecard has no score below 3.
